extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary readers, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on what constitutes good poetry and how poets should write, with criteria about expression, form, clarity, imagery, and the moral/aesthetic function of poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and restraint in expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should 'embody the soul's higher and purer emotions in the simplest and directest terms which the language affords' and should avoid excessive intensity of expression, vehemence of epithet, volcanic passion, and a profusion of superlatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit anti-pattern: the Byronic excesses of overwrought passion and superlatives are 'out of place' in true poetry. The essay cites Wordsworth's deliberate protest against excessive intensity as a wholesome corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, lucidity, and directness
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poetry should be simple, lucid, and straightforward; avoid speaking in riddles or unnecessary obscurity that bars the average reader from comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated criticism of modern literature 'lacking simplicity, lucidity, straightforwardness.' Browning's perceived obscurity is used as an example of failing clarity; anti-patterns include piling fancies in wild confusion and demanding many re-readings to grasp meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of inspiration / necessity to write
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should write from the 'spur of thoughts burning for expression' — from genuine inspiration — not for commercial motives (i.e., not to 'write Poetry for potatoes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay holds that writing primarily for money dilutes poetry; anecdotes about poets who wrote for livelihood versus those who wrote from inner necessity are used to support valuing authentic motive over pecuniary aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful craftsmanship, polish, and editorial restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems should show evident labor and extreme polish; authors should practice restraint (write sparingly rather than overproduce) and avoid diluting quality by excessive output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tennyson is praised for carefulness and 'extreme polish' and for producing a moderate body of work despite long career. The text warns of the temptation to 'overwrite' when fame or publishers offer rewards; 'not to dilute his nectar' is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery, musicality, and felicitous expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellent poetry is 'rich and pure in imagery,' 'dainty and felicitous in expression,' and 'musical and mellifluous in rhythm and cadence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tennyson's minor poems are cited as exemplars of these qualities. Guidance implies attention to choice of images, euphony, and rhythmic control as measures of poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent organization and control of fancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should organize its materials coherently; a poet's ideas and fancies must be 'well stowed' so they do not rush forth in a chaotic, confusing mass that chokes meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browning's weakness is diagnosed as a failure of arrangement: 'his fancies are piled one upon another in wild confusion' and later writings are 'half spoiled by this chaotic whirl.' Anti-pattern: unchecked piling of images/ideas without structural control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's transcendent function
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's proper office is to 'lift the soul above the region of mere sense,' apprehend truth in its universal character and all-pervading relations, and thereby exalt and purify the reader's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative definition of what poetry must aim to accomplish (its aesthetic/moral purpose) rather than a formal rule. Examples include poetic renderings of Creation and the immortality of mental creations, showing superiority over plain prose in spiritual effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness and intensified presentation of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetic statement should present truths with greater vividness and force than plain prose, making the idea more immediate and affecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative quotations (e.g., Job's speech from the whirlwind, Byron's lines on beings of the mind, and lines about thunder leaping from crag to crag) are cited as examples where poetry fuses a thought into more vivid, forceful expression than prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal flexibility: do not equate poetry with metre or rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse, metre, and rhyme are not essential to Poetry; poetry may be prose — the form (rhymed or metrical verse) does not alone constitute poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cautions against the common delusion that equates Poetry with Verse (i.e., rhyme). Examples: Chateaubriand and Willis wrote great poetic prose; rhyme likely originates later than poetry itself. Anti-pattern: assuming capitalized, metered, rhymed lines are inherently poetry.
